blocks.content: The SQL Fundamentals module covered SELECT, WHERE, and the other core building blocks of a single query. This new module, SQL Filtering and Aggregation, opens with GROUP BY, the clause that genuinely changes how a query thinks about rows, collapsing many individual rows into one summary row per group.

This topic covers what GROUP BY actually does, why every selected column genuinely must be either grouped or aggregated, grouping by more than one column at once, and how this all sets up HAVING, covered directly afterward, which filters the grouped results GROUP BY actually produces.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035281342-162328515.png
blocks.alt: SQL GROUP BY opens the SQL Filtering and Aggregation module by collapsing many rows into one summary row per group

blocks.content: 1. Without GROUP BY Versus With GROUP BY
blocks.text: 1. Without GROUP BY Versus With GROUP BY

blocks.content: A table of individual order rows, queried without GROUP BY, shows every single order separately, one row per actual order that exists in the table, regardless of how many orders happen to share the same department.
The same table, queried with GROUP BY department, shows one summary row per department instead, collapsing every order within a given department down into a single row representing that entire group.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035283237-177995790.png
blocks.alt: Without GROUP BY, every order row is shown separately; with GROUP BY department, one summary row represents each department

blocks.content: 2. What GROUP BY Actually Does

GROUP BY genuinely buckets rows that share the same value in a specified column, every row with department equal to Engineering goes into one bucket, every row with department equal to Sales goes into another, and so on for every distinct value present.

It then collapses each bucket down to a single summary row. GROUP BY genuinely requires an aggregate function, like COUNT or SUM, to actually be useful, since the summary row needs some way to represent the many original rows it collapsed, and an aggregate function is exactly that mechanism.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035284873-190247441.png
blocks.alt: GROUP BY buckets rows sharing the same column value, collapses each bucket to one summary row, and genuinely requires an aggregate function to be useful

3. A Worked Example
A concrete query shows GROUP BY applied to a real, common question. An orders table has a department column, and a specific query needs to know how many orders each department actually placed.
SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY department;
blocks.code: SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY department;

codes.sql: SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY department;

blocks.content: This query returns exactly one row per department, each with its own order count, genuinely answering how many orders each department placed, without you having to manually count through every individual order row yourself.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035286485-804061510.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: an orders table grouped by department, returning one row per department with its own order count

blocks.content: 4. Every Selected Column Genuinely Needs a Reason
blocks.text: 4. Every Selected Column Genuinely Needs a Reason

blocks.content: Selecting a column that is neither in the GROUP BY list nor wrapped in an aggregate function is genuinely ambiguous, since a single summary row represents many original rows, and if those original rows had different values in that ungrouped column, the database has no real, well defined way to pick which one to actually show.

Selecting a column that is either grouped or aggregated is genuinely well defined, since a grouped column has exactly one shared value across the entire group by definition, and an aggregated column produces exactly one computed value summarizing the whole group.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035288048-281809653.png
blocks.alt: A selected column not grouped or aggregated is genuinely ambiguous; a column that is either grouped or aggregated is genuinely well defined

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Selecting a column that is neither in the GROUP BY list nor wrapped in an aggregate function. Many databases reject this outright with an error, while some silently pick an arbitrary value, either way it is a genuinely real mistake worth avoiding deliberately.
5. Grouping by More Than One Column
blocks.text: 5. Grouping by More Than One Column

blocks.content: GROUP BY genuinely supports grouping by more than one column at once, where each unique combination of values across those columns becomes its own distinct group, not just each unique value in a single column.

GROUP BY department, role groups rows by the combination of department and role together, producing one row per department and role combination that actually exists, engineering managers grouped separately from engineering individual contributors, even though both share the same department.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035289603-110755396.png
blocks.alt: Grouping by more than one column treats each unique combination as its own group, like department and role together

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Every column listed in GROUP BY genuinely narrows what counts as one group. Adding a second column to GROUP BY generally produces more, smaller groups, not fewer, larger ones.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine GROUP BY usage. Selecting a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated, producing a genuinely ambiguous or outright rejected query. Forgetting that GROUP BY runs before SELECT genuinely computes its columns, part of the real SQL execution order covered earlier in this course.

And trying to filter an aggregate value directly with WHERE instead of HAVING, which fails since WHERE runs before GROUP BY has even computed those aggregates, exactly the reason HAVING exists as its own separate clause, covered directly in the next topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035291391-719919434.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: selecting an ungrouped, unaggregated column, forgetting GROUP BY runs before SELECT, and using WHERE instead of HAVING for aggregates

Using WHERE to filter a computed aggregate value: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, use HAVING instead for that purpose.
